title: Chapter 19 — Some Observations On The Drama Amongst Democratic Nations
paragraphs: When the revolution that overturns the social and political state of an aristocratic people begins to reach literature, it generally shows itself first in the drama, and it always remains most conspicuous there. The spectator of a dramatic piece is, to some degree, caught off guard by the impression it produces. He has no time to consult his memory or to ask those better able to judge than he is. It does not occur to him to resist the new literary tendencies he begins to feel; he yields to them before he knows what they are. Authors are very quick to detect which way the public's taste is thus secretly leaning. They shape their productions accordingly, and the literature of the stage, after serving as an indicator of the coming literary revolution, quickly completes it. If you want to judge in advance the literature of a people sliding into democracy, study its dramatic productions.

The literature of the stage, moreover, even among aristocratic nations, is the most democratic part of their literature. No kind of literary enjoyment is so accessible to the multitude as that drawn from theatrical performances. Neither preparation nor study is required to enjoy them; they seize you in the midst of your prejudices and your ignorance. When the still untutored love of the pleasures of the mind begins to touch a class of the community, it draws that class instantly toward the stage. The theaters of aristocratic nations have always been filled with spectators who do not belong to the aristocracy. In the theater alone do the upper ranks mix with the middle and lower classes; there alone do they consent to listen to the opinion of those below them, or at least allow them to give an opinion at all. At the theater, men of cultivation and literary accomplishment have always had more difficulty than elsewhere in making their taste prevail over that of the people, or in keeping themselves from being carried along by it. The pit has often made laws for the boxes.

If it is difficult for an aristocracy to keep the people from gaining the upper hand in the theater, it will easily be understood that the people will be supreme there once democratic principles have crept into the laws and customs — when ranks are mingled, when minds as well as fortunes are brought closer together, and when the upper class has lost, along with its hereditary wealth, its power, its precedents, and its leisure. The tastes and tendencies natural to democratic nations in literature will therefore appear first in the drama, and it can be foreseen that they will break out there with force. In written works, the literary canons of aristocracy will be gently, gradually, and, so to speak, legally modified; in the theater they will be riotously overthrown. The drama brings out most of the good qualities, and almost all the defects, inherent in democratic literature. Democratic peoples hold erudition very cheap and care little for what happened in Rome and Athens; they want to hear something that concerns themselves, and the portrayal of the present age is what they demand.

When the heroes and manners of antiquity are frequently brought upon the stage, and dramatic authors faithfully observe the rules of old precedent, that alone is enough to conclude that the democratic classes have not yet gained the upper hand over the theaters. Racine makes a very humble apology in the preface to Britannicus for having placed Junia among the Vestals, who, according to Aulus Gellius, he says, "admitted no one below the age of six or above ten." We may be sure he would neither have accused himself of the offense nor defended himself against censure if he had been writing for our contemporaries. A fact of this kind illustrates not only the state of literature at the time it occurred, but also the state of society itself. A democratic stage does not prove that the nation is in a state of democracy; for, as we have just seen, even in aristocracies democratic tastes may affect the drama. But when the spirit of aristocracy reigns exclusively on the stage, the fact irrefutably shows that society as a whole is aristocratic, and one may boldly conclude that the same lettered and learned class that sways the dramatic writers also commands the people and governs the country.

The refined tastes and the arrogant bearing of an aristocracy will rarely fail to lead it, when it controls the stage, to make a kind of selection within human nature. Some conditions of society claim its chief interest, and the scenes that depict their manners are preferred on the stage. Certain virtues, and even certain vices, are thought more especially to deserve a place there, and they are applauded while all the others are excluded. On the stage, as elsewhere, an aristocratic audience will meet only persons of quality and share the emotions of kings. The same applies to style: an aristocracy is apt to impose on dramatic authors certain modes of expression that set the key in which everything must be delivered. By these means the stage often comes to depict only one side of man, or sometimes even to represent what is not to be found in human nature at all — to rise above nature and go beyond it.

In democratic communities the spectators have no such preferences, and they rarely show any such antipathies. They like to see upon the stage that mixture of conditions, feelings, and opinions which occurs before their eyes. The drama becomes more striking, more common, and more true. Sometimes, however, those who write for the stage in democracies also overstep the bounds of human nature — but on a different side from their predecessors. By trying to depict in minute detail the small peculiarities of the moment and the particular features of certain characters, they forget to portray the general features of the race.

When the democratic classes rule the stage, they introduce as much license in the way subjects are treated as in the choice of them. Since the love of drama is, of all literary tastes, the most natural to democratic nations, the number of authors, spectators, and theatrical performances constantly increases among these communities. A multitude made up of such different elements, scattered in so many different places, cannot acknowledge the same rules or submit to the same laws. No agreement is possible among so many judges, who do not know when they may meet again, so each pronounces his own verdict on the piece. If the general effect of democracy is to question the authority of all literary rules and conventions, on the stage it abolishes them altogether and puts in their place nothing but the whim of each author and each public.

The drama also displays in a particular way the truth of what I have said earlier about style and art in democratic literature more generally. Reading the criticisms provoked by the dramatic productions of the age of Louis XIV, one is surprised to notice the great stress the public laid on the probability of the plot, and the importance attached to the perfect consistency of the characters and to their doing nothing that could not be easily explained and understood. The value placed on the forms of language in that period, and the petty quarrels about words with which dramatic authors were assailed, are no less surprising. It seems the men of the age of Louis XIV attached exaggerated importance to details that may be noticed in the study but escape attention on the stage. For after all, the chief purpose of a dramatic piece is to be performed, and its chief merit is to move the audience. But audience and readers in that age were the same people: on leaving the theater they summoned the author to judgment at their own firesides. In democracies dramatic pieces are listened to, but not read. Most of those who frequent the amusements of the stage do not go there to seek the pleasures of the mind, but the keen emotions of the heart. They do not expect to hear a fine literary work, but to see a play. As long as the author writes his country's language correctly enough to be understood, and his characters stir curiosity and awaken sympathy, the audience is satisfied. They ask no more of fiction and return immediately to real life. Accuracy of style is therefore less required, because a careful observance of its rules is less noticeable on the stage. As for probability of plot, it is incompatible with perpetual novelty, surprise, and rapidity of invention. It is therefore neglected, and the public excuses the neglect. You may be sure that if you succeed in bringing your audience into the presence of something that moves them, they will not care by what road you brought them there, and they will never reproach you for having stirred their emotions in spite of dramatic rules.

The Americans display very broadly all the different tendencies I have just described when they go to the theater. But it must be admitted that as yet very few of them go to theaters at all. Although playgoers and plays have increased prodigiously in the United States over the last forty years, the population indulges this kind of amusement with the greatest reserve. This is due to special causes the reader already knows, of which a few words will suffice as a reminder. The Puritans who founded the American republics were not only enemies of amusements; they professed a special abhorrence of the stage. They regarded it as an abominable pastime, and as long as their principles held undivided sway, theatrical performances were wholly unknown among them. These opinions of the first fathers of the colony have left very deep marks on the minds of their descendants. The extreme regularity of habits and the great strictness of manners in the United States have so far raised further obstacles to the growth of dramatic art. There are no dramatic subjects in a country that has witnessed no great political catastrophes, and in which love invariably leads by a straight and easy road to matrimony. People who spend every day of the week making money, and Sunday going to church, offer nothing to invite the muse of Comedy.

A single fact is enough to show that the stage is not very popular in the United States. The Americans, whose laws allow the utmost freedom and even license of language in every other respect, have nonetheless subjected their dramatic authors to a kind of censorship. Theatrical performances can only take place with the permission of the municipal authorities. This helps show how much communities resemble individuals: they surrender without scruple to their ruling passions, and afterwards take the greatest care not to yield too much to the force of tastes they do not possess.

No branch of literature is tied by closer or more numerous bonds to the present state of society than the drama. The drama of one period can never suit the next, if in the meantime an important revolution has changed the manners and the laws of the nation. The great authors of an earlier age may still be read, but pieces written for a different public will not be followed. The dramatic authors of the past survive only in books. The traditional taste of certain individuals, together with vanity, fashion, or the genius of an actor, may sustain or revive for a time the aristocratic drama in a democracy. But it will quickly fade away on its own — not overthrown, but abandoned.
